evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Languages with fixed word order (e.g., English) and explicit case marking (e.g., German) the speed of deductive reasoning tasks that require syntactic parsing of nested relative clauses, with the constraint being weaker in case-marked languages due to reduced ambiguity]

[PATH:empirical] Cross-linguistic reading-time experiments comparing nested relative clause processing in English vs. German (e.g., using self-paced reading or eye-tracking) — Directly tests whether case marking reduces syntactic ambiguity and thus speeds deductive reasoning involving nested clauses. Comparing English (fixed word order, no case) and German (fixed word order, explicit case) provides a clean contrast.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of psycholinguistic studies on case-marking and garden-path effects (e.g., papers by Bader & Meng, or by Levy & Keller) — Synthesizes existing evidence on how case marking affects parsing difficulty and ambiguity resolution, which underpins the hypothesized constraint on deductive reasoning speed.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of deductive reasoning with a parser that incorporates case-marking cues (e.g., using ACT-R or surprisal-based models) — Simulates the predicted speed difference under varying ambiguity and case-marking conditions, providing a mechanistic account that can be tested against empirical data.

scope.domain: syntactic parsing efficiency and case-marking effects in deductive reasoning

qualifier.geographic: English-speaking and German-speaking populations in Western Europe and North America

[PATH:empirical] Controlled behavioral experiments comparing deductive reasoning accuracy and response times between native speakers of Latin/Finnish and speakers of configurational languages (e.g., English) on syntactically ambiguous syllogisms — Directly tests whether morphological processing load (e.g., case-marking resolution) imposes additional working memory demands that impair reasoning efficiency, by measuring performance differences under controlled syntactic complexity.

[PATH:empirical] Neuroimaging studies (e.g., fMRI or EEG) examining working memory activation patterns (e.g., in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) during deductive reasoning tasks in Latin/Finnish speakers vs. speakers of configurational languages — Provides neural evidence for increased cognitive load during syntactic parsing in rich case-marking languages, linking morphological processing to working memory resource depletion.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of parsing and reasoning (e.g., incremental parser models combined with ACT-R working memory constraints) simulating the effect of case-marking complexity on deductive inference accuracy — Enables quantitative predictions about the hypothesized impairment, allowing comparison with empirical data and isolating the role of morphological vs. syntactic cueing in reasoning.
